title: Quantized Attention Regularization for Fair LLMs
one_liner: Stop large language models from encoding social biases by injecting structured quantization into their attention layers, without fine-tuning the model.
lead: Large language models learn to recognize patterns in text, including harmful social stereotypes tied to race, gender, and other sensitive features. Existing debiasing methods are expensive (they need to retrain parts of the model), inflexible (they work only on specific model architectures), and incomplete (they ignore where much of the bias is encoded: in the layers that learn to focus on different parts of text). This paper proposes MQAR, a method that surgically quiets bias in the focusing mechanism without retraining the model backbone.

problem.h2: Language models learn the world's prejudices
paras: A large language model is a pattern-matching engine. It reads billions of text examples and learns which words tend to follow which other words. When people write text that contains stereotypes, the model learns those stereotypes too. So when you ask it questions about job candidates or characteristics, it can produce answers biased by race, gender, age, or disability.

Existing debiasing methods have three problems. First, they require expensive fine-tuning—retraining parts or all of the model on carefully chosen data, which is slow and costs money. Second, they only work on specific model architectures, so a new model architecture breaks them. Third, they focus only on the input (what you type in) or the output (what the model types out), while ignoring the middle layers where much of the bias lives. A beginner might try to just filter the model's outputs, but that does not fix the bias—it just hides it, and the model still makes biased predictions if you ask it a slightly different way.

callout.html: Social biases are learned and encoded deep inside the model, but existing fixes are expensive, inflexible, and incomplete.

steps.text: Do not retrain any core weights; keep the model exactly as is.

steps.b: Attach a quantization layer to attention
steps.text: Insert a learnable discretizer (vector quantization) inside frozen attention layers.

steps.b: Round continuous attention values to discrete codes
steps.text: Quantization forces smooth attention signals into sharp, bounded bins; stereotypical patterns get erased.
Train a small classifier to detect if the quantized activations still leak protected-attribute information.
Push quantization to erase protected-attribute clues while the discriminator pulls back; find the equilibrium.

paras: The paper modifies the internal activations inside the attention mechanism—the continuously-valued signals that flow through the model when it reads and focuses on text. It does not retrain the model weights. Instead, it adds a learned quantizer (a function that rounds numbers) that transforms those activations into discrete codes, and then an adversarial classifier that suppresses any remaining bias signals.

hidden.name: protected-attribute signal strength
paras: Protected-attribute leakage is how much the model's internal attention activations still contain clues about a person's race, gender, or other sensitive feature. If activations are heavily biased, they leak a strong signal; if quantization has erased the bias, they leak a weak signal. The paper measures this by training a small discriminator classifier on the quantized activations—if the discriminator can still accurately predict gender or race from those activations, leakage is high; if it cannot, leakage is low.

MQAR uses the discriminator loss as a signal: a penalty that punishes activations still carrying protected-attribute information. The goal is to make the discriminator fail—to force the activations into a form where no classifier can extract demographic clues.

heat.caption: Darker cells carry stronger gender/race signals; MQAR pushes all toward light (neutral).

reads.html: The discriminator is like a lie detector for bias. If your attention activations still whisper 'woman' or 'Black' to someone who listens carefully, the discriminator hears it and complains. MQAR turns up the penalty until the activations stop whispering.

The paper estimates protected-attribute leakage via a discriminator-guided adversarial loss over the quantized activations. Minimizing this loss forces activations into regions that are provably harder to decode for demographic prediction.

paras: Bias lives in the continuous, fine-grained details inside the model. A model learns tiny, delicate patterns: slightly stronger activation for 'man', slightly weaker for 'woman', compounded across millions of numbers. These fine details encode stereotypes perfectly because they encode everything—they have infinite resolution.

Quantization is a sledgehammer: it rounds all those continuous values into a small set of discrete bins. Instead of 1.0, 1.001, 0.999, 0.998, 0.997—each encoding a different bias flavor—quantization says 'you can only be 0, 1, 2, or 3'. This kills the fine gradations that bias depends on. A stereotypical pattern that relied on 18 subtle variations across 50 weights cannot hide in a 4-bin world.

The adversarial discriminator amplifies this. After quantization, MQAR trains a separate classifier: 'Can you guess the protected attribute from these quantized activations?' If the answer is yes, MQAR adjusts the quantizer further (making bins even more neutral, or moving the bin boundaries). If the answer is no, MQAR stops. The result: the model's internal representations become demonstrably insensitive to protected attributes.

stages.s: If yes, shift bins further neutral; re-optimize

math.words: The total loss is the task loss plus a weighted penalty for protected-attribute leakage. The penalty measures the discriminator's accuracy at guessing the protected attribute from quantized activations; MQAR minimizes this penalty.
symbols: original task loss (e.g., predicting the next word)
weight controlling fairness strength (bigger = more debiasing)
loss when training discriminator to guess protected attribute
the discretized activation vectors after rounding

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose L_task = 0.8 (small, good predictions) and lambda = 1.0.
Discriminator initially achieves 92% accuracy (high leakage): L_discriminator = 0.08.
MQAR adjusts the quantizer bins; discriminator accuracy drops to 52%: L_discriminator = 0.48.
New total loss: L = 0.8 + 1.0 * 0.48 = 1.28 (higher, but fairness improved).
If lambda is smaller (e.g., 0.1), the model cares less about fairness and L stays low. Bigger lambda forces fairness.

math.note: The min-max game: quantization shrinks leakage, the discriminator hunts for remaining leakage, and MQAR keeps adjusting until equilibrium is reached.

bars.h2: Impact on bias and task accuracy

charts.title: Baseline model (before debiasing)
charts.note: High bias, but task performance is strong. The trade-off is the problem.

charts.title: After MQAR debiasing
charts.note: Bias halved, accuracy barely dents (0.2% drop). No expensive retraining needed.

items.html: If you use only 2 or 3 discrete bins, the model cannot make fine distinctions even for the task. Downstream accuracy drops sharply. The fix: tune the number of bins per layer, balancing debiasing and task performance.

items.b: Discriminator is too weak to detect remaining bias.
items.html: If the discriminator is a simple linear classifier, it might miss subtle correlations in the quantized activations, because a weak classifier cannot see fine patterns. Bias persists even if the discriminator says it does not. Fix: use a more complex discriminator (e.g., a deeper neural network with more layers) or train multiple discriminators hunting for different protected attributes.

A model can be fair on gender alone and fair on race alone, but still biased on the combination (e.g., 'Black women'). If you only train one discriminator per attribute, intersectional bias survives. Fix: explicitly add discriminators for attribute pairs and intersections.
Tune lambda, the quantization bits, and the discriminator strength together. Validate on multi-attribute benchmarks like CrowS-Pairs. Check downstream accuracy on the real tasks you care about.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small language model (e.g., a BERT variant or GPT-Neo-small) on a gender-biased text corpus. Add MQAR quantization to one or two focusing layers. Train a discriminator to predict 'male' or 'female' from the quantized internal signals. Measure how much the quantizer needs to erase before the discriminator cannot guess better than random coin-flip accuracy (50%), because a random guess right-or-wrong is the true baseline for 'forget the attribute'. Compare the internal signals before and after: show that fine-grained gender cues disappear but the model still completes sentences correctly. Measure downstream task accuracy before and after MQAR to confirm the trade-off is tiny.
demo.closing: The demo must make clear that quantization erases bias in the attention layer without requiring any model retraining, and that the cost in task accuracy is tiny.
